title: Be still (Psalm 45 [46])
hook: mountains fall into the sea, and God says be still and see that I am God

segments.voice: Yesterday, as the hart panteth: a soul thirsty for God, talking gently to its own sadness. Your line was why art thou sad, my soul. Today, a psalm with an earthquake in it.

The words turn up on mugs and wall prints, in soft script over a calm lake: be still. It looks like a spa slogan. Breathe. Relax. Light a candle. But go back to where the line comes from, and there's no calm lake anywhere. The ground is shaking. Mountains are sliding into the ocean. The sea is roaring. Nations are at war. And right in the middle of all that noise, God speaks.
screen: `A MUG WITH A CALM LAKE.` → `THE REAL SETTING: EARTHQUAKE.` → `GOD SPEAKS IN THE NOISE.`

segments.voice: Psalm 45 in the Douay, 46 in most Bibles, opens: "Our God is our refuge and strength: a helper in troubles, which have found us exceedingly." Troubles that found us, as if they came looking. Then the disaster: "Therefore we will not fear, when the earth shall be troubled; and the mountains shall be removed into the heart of the sea." The solid ground itself gives way. And in the middle of the chaos, a quiet picture: "The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful." Jerusalem had no great river. The psalm gives it one anyway, a gentle stream that makes a city glad while the sea rages. Then God speaks. He makes wars cease to the ends of the earth, breaks the bow, burns the shields. And then: "Be still and see that I am God." Here's the surprise. The Hebrew word behind be still is usually rendered let go: relax your grip, stop. It's less a spa word than a word you'd shout at two armies: enough, put it down. The Latin Bible put it as vacate: be free, make room. So the line is a command to stop fighting, stop grasping, stop trying to hold the mountains up yourself, and see who God is. In this psalm, stillness isn't what you do once life is calm. It's what you do while it isn't.
screen: `MOUNTAINS INTO THE SEA.` · `A RIVER MAKES THE CITY GLAD.` · `BE STILL: LET GO, DROP YOUR HANDS.` · `VACATE: BE FREE, MAKE ROOM.`

segments.voice: For sixty seconds, be still, not calm, just still: let your hands drop into your lap, palms open, as if you've just put something heavy down. Notice what's shaking in your life right now; you don't have to fix any of it for this minute, just stop holding it up. If you pray, hear the line as God's word to you, be still and see that I am God; if you don't, simply let your hands stay open.
Be still. In the psalm, not a spa word but a command in the middle of chaos: let go, drop your hands, and see. Today's word.
Your line: be still and see. The mountains were never yours to hold up. Day one hundred seventy, done.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 45 [46] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at Mass, including on the feast of the Dedication of the Lateran Basilica, where the river that makes the city of God glad is read alongside images of the Temple.

notes: Douay Psalm 45 wording (verses 2, 3, 5, 11): confirm against a Challoner edition.
Hebrew harpu (hiphil of raphah): let go, relax, desist. Vulgate 'vacate et videte'. Confirm.
Jerusalem's lack of a great river: the Gihon spring is its water source; 'no great river' is a fair simplification. Confirm.
howItsDone: Psalm 46 is the responsorial psalm for the Dedication of the Lateran Basilica (November 9). Confirm.
